subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will sort and organise things. You will put objects into sets using one rule, explain the rule you chose in your own words, count and compare your sets to say which has more, and use a sorting circle — a Venn diagram — including the middle part where things belong to both groups.

outcomes: Sort a group of objects into two sets using one rule (for example red / not red).
Explain the sorting rule they used in their own words.
Understand that a set is a group of things that belong together.
Count how many objects are in each set and answer how-many questions.
Compare two sets and say which has more and which has fewer.
Notice that the same objects can be sorted in different ways.
Understand that a Venn diagram is a sorting circle: things that fit go inside, things that do not stay outside.
Sort objects into a one-circle Venn diagram, and take first steps with two overlapping circles (the middle means both).
A pile of small objects to sort: buttons, dates, stones, bottle caps, beads, or dry beans in mixed colours and sizes.

concepts.title: What Is a Set? (sorting by one rule)
concepts.explanation: A set is simply a group of things that belong together because they share something – they are all red, all round, all animals, or all toys. Sorting is the act of putting objects into sets. This is the foundation of the whole unit, so spend the most time here with real objects you can touch and move. How to teach it: Tip a small pile of buttons onto a mat. Say, ‘Let us put all the red ones here and all the not-red ones here.’ Move the first two or three yourself, thinking out loud, then continue. When they finish, ask the key question: ‘Why do these belong together?’ Getting you to say the rule – ‘they are all red’ – matters more than the sorting itself. Always sort into two sets first: the things that fit the rule, and the things that do not (‘red’ and ‘not red’). This ‘something / not something’ pairing is the clearest way in for a five-year-old. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Look at all these buttons. Let us sort them. Put the red buttons in this pile.” Child sorts. You: “Now, why do all these belong together?” Child: “They are all red!” You: “Yes! This is a set of red buttons. And these over here are the not-red buttons.” Sort many different things across the week – buttons by colour, toys into soft and hard, fruit and vegetables, stones into big and small. The more varied the objects, the more you understand that sorting works for anything. Keep the language steady and simple: sort, set, same, different. Say these words often so they become your own.
concepts.example: One powerful idea to plant gently: the same objects can be sorted in more than one way. Sort the buttons by colour, then sweep them back together and sort the very same buttons by size. You begins to see that a sorting rule is a choice, not a fixed property of the objects. This is a genuinely important mathematical idea and children find it delightful once they notice it.

concepts.title: Counting and Comparing Sets (more / fewer)
concepts.explanation: Once objects are sorted into two sets, the natural next question is ‘How many are in each?’ and ‘Which set has more?’ This links your counting skills from earlier units to the new idea of comparing groups. How to teach it: After sorting, count each set aloud together, touching each object once, and say the total: ‘This set has 5. This set has 3.’ Then compare: ‘5 is more than 3, so the set of red buttons has more.’ For the surest comparison, line the two sets up and match one object from each into pairs. The set with objects left over is the one with more. This matching method is more reliable than looking, because a few big objects can look like ‘more’ even when a set of small objects actually has a greater number. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us count. How many red buttons?” Child and you: “One, two, three, four, five.” You: “And how many blue buttons?” Child: “One, two, three.” You: “Five and three. Which is more?” Child: “Five!” You: “Yes – the red set has more, the blue set has fewer.”
concepts.example: Helps you understand that the size of the objects does not decide which set has more – only the number of objects does. Three big stones is fewer than five little dates, even though the stones take up more room. Compare sets with different-sized objects on purpose so you learn to trust counting and matching over a quick glance.

concepts.title: The Venn Diagram — One Sorting Circle
concepts.explanation: A Venn diagram is just a sorting circle. Things that fit the rule go inside the circle; things that do not fit stay outside. Because you have already been sorting into ‘something / not something’, a one-circle Venn diagram is a small, natural step: the circle is the ‘something’ pile, and outside is the ‘not something’ pile. How to teach it: Make a big circle on the floor or table with a loop of string. Say, ‘Inside this circle we will put all the animals.’ Give you a mix of toy animals and other objects and place each one inside or outside. Then count: ‘How many are inside? How many are outside?’ Using a real loop of string that you can place objects into makes the idea concrete before it ever appears on paper.
concepts.example: 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “This circle is for red things. Where does the red ball go?” Child places it inside. You: “Where does the blue cup go?” Child: “Outside – it is not red.” You: “Well done. Inside is for red things. Outside is for everything that is not red.”

concepts.title: Two Circles and the Middle (‘both’)
concepts.explanation: This is the newest and trickiest idea, so treat it as a gentle first taste rather than something to master. Make two circles that overlap with two loops of string. One circle is for ‘toys’, the other for ‘red things’. An object that is a toy and red – a red teddy – belongs in the middle, where the circles overlap, because it fits both rules at once. How to teach it: Start by placing objects that clearly fit only one circle – a blue car is a toy but not red, an apple is red but not a toy. Then bring out the red teddy and ask, ‘This is a toy AND it is red. Where can it go?’ puzzle over it, then show how the overlapping middle solves the problem. Objects that fit neither rule (a green cup) go outside both circles. Keep to a few very clear objects. The aim is only that you meet the idea that the middle means ‘both’; deep mastery comes in later years. Thinking objects can only be sorted one way. The same pile can be sorted by colour, then by size, then by type. Re-sort the very same objects a different way to show this. Believing the arrangement makes the set. A set is defined by its rule, not by how the objects are laid out. Spread a set out, bunch it up, and show it is still the same set. Thinking bigger objects mean ‘more’. Only the number of objects decides which set has more. Compare a few big items with many small ones and count to check.
concepts.example: In a Venn diagram, believing an object can only go in one circle. An object with two matching features belongs in the overlapping middle – it can be in ‘both’.

concepts.title: What This Unit Is About: Sorting and Comparing
concepts.explanation:
This unit is your first taste of statistics — the maths of organising information so you can understand it.

At this age that means three friendly ideas. The first is sorting: putting objects that are alike into the same group, which we call a set. You choose a rule for your sorting, such as colour or shape, and the rule decides which set each object belongs to.

The second idea is comparing your sets. Once things are sorted you can count each set and say which has more and which has fewer.

The third idea is the sorting circle, called a Venn diagram. Things that follow the rule go inside the circle, and things that do not go outside it. With two circles, anything that belongs to both sets sits in the middle where the circles overlap.
concepts.example: Sort a pile of buttons into red buttons and buttons that are not red. Count each set. Say which set has more and which has fewer.

concepts.title: Choosing a Good Sorting Rule
concepts.explanation: A sorting rule should be clear enough that anyone could use it and get the same two groups every time — for example, red vs. Not red, or round vs. Not round. Pick one property at a time. If you try to sort by two things at once (red AND round), some objects will not fit neatly into either group, which is confusing. Practising with a pile of buttons or beads: choose one clear rule, sort every object into one of two sets, then explain the rule out loud.
concepts.example: A pile of mixed buttons: some are red, some are blue, some are yellow. The rule ‘red / not red’ gives two clear sets. If a button is red AND round, it still only needs to answer one question — is it red? — to know which set it belongs in.

explorations.title: What Is a Set? (sorting by one rule)
explorations.context: A set is simply a group of things that belong together because they share something – they are all red, all round, all animals, or all toys. Sorting is the act of putting objects into sets.
explorations.prompt: If you sort a pile of buttons into a 'red' pile and a 'not red' pile, what do all the buttons in the 'red' pile have in common?
explorations.hint: Look only at the buttons in that one pile — what is the same about every single one?
explorations.explanation: The point is not the sorting itself but the naming: once the two piles are made, ask ‘why do these belong together?’ and helps you turn the answer into one short sentence, such as ‘they are all red.’ Praise the sentence as much as the sorting, because explaining the rule out loud is what turns a physical task into a mathematical one.

explorations.title: Counting and Comparing Sets (more / fewer)
explorations.context: Once objects are sorted into two sets, the natural next question is ‘How many are in each?’ and ‘Which set has more?’ This links your counting skills from earlier units to the new idea of comparing groups.
explorations.prompt: You count 5 red buttons and 3 blue buttons. Which set has more?
explorations.answer: The red buttons (5 is more than 3).
explorations.hint: Match one red button to one blue button in pairs — whichever set has buttons left over has more.
explorations.explanation: Counting each set separately answers ‘how many,’ but matching one object from each set into pairs is what makes ‘more’ and ‘fewer’ certain rather than a guess — whichever set has objects left over with no partner is the one with more. Point at the leftover objects as their proof when they say which set has more.

explorations.title: The Venn Diagram — One Sorting Circle
explorations.context: A Venn diagram is just a sorting circle. Things that fit the rule go inside the circle; things that do not fit stay outside.
explorations.prompt: A circle is drawn for the rule 'red things'. A red ball and a blue cup are nearby. Which one goes inside the circle?
explorations.hint: Check whether each object matches the rule written for the circle.
explorations.explanation: A loop of string or a hoop makes the circle real and touchable, which matters more at this age than a diagram drawn on paper. Once you can place several objects correctly, ask them to explain the rule for the circle in your own words — ‘because it's red’ — so the picture and the reasoning stay connected.

explorations.title: Two Circles and the Middle (‘both’)
explorations.context: This is the newest and trickiest idea, so treat it as a gentle first taste rather than something to master. Make two circles that overlap with two loops of string. One circle is for ‘toys’, the other for ‘red things’.
explorations.prompt: Two circles overlap: one for 'toys' and one for 'red things'. Where does a red toy teddy go?
explorations.answer: In the middle, where the two circles overlap.
explorations.hint: Ask: is it a toy? Is it also red? If both are true, it belongs where the circles overlap.
explorations.explanation: Sit with the puzzle for a moment before showing the answer — most children want to put the red teddy in just one circle, and that hesitation is a good sign they are thinking hard about the rule. Only after they have tried does it help to show that the overlapping middle is a place that satisfies both rules at once, not a compromise between them.

explorations.title: Unit 7 is your first taste
explorations.context: Unit 7 is your first taste of statistics – the maths of organising and comparing information.
explorations.prompt: When you get a new pile of objects, which comes first: sorting them into sets, or counting how many are in each set?
explorations.answer: Sorting them into sets comes first.
explorations.hint: Think about what you need to do before you can count how many are in each pile.
explorations.explanation: These three ideas build on each other in order: sorting comes first because a set only exists once a rule has been named, counting and comparing come next because numbers give the sets meaning, and the Venn diagram comes last because it is simply a new picture for the same ‘something / not something’ thinking you have already practised. Keep circling back to real objects rather than worksheets — the whole unit is easiest to grasp with things you can pick up and move.

explorations.title: Sort a group of objects into two
explorations.context: Sort a group of objects into two sets using one rule (for example red / not red).
explorations.prompt: You have a pile of buttons that are red and blue. What is one simple rule you could use to sort them into two sets?
explorations.hint: Pick one feature, like colour, and ask 'does it fit — yes or no?'
explorations.explanation: Always sort into two sets first — the things that fit the rule, and the things that do not — because this ‘something / not something’ pairing is the clearest way in for a five-year-old, before any more complex sorting is attempted. Move the objects themselves rather than just watching, since physically placing each item into a pile is what fixes the rule in their mind.

methods.title: Sorting a Pile by One Rule
methods.example: Tip out a pile of dried beans and sort them into 'brown' and 'not brown'.
steps: Tip a small pile of objects, such as dried beans, onto the mat in front of you.
Choose one clear rule together, like 'brown / not brown', and say it out loud before starting.
Move each object into one of the two piles, checking it against the rule as you go.

methods.title: Explaining the Sorting Rule
methods.example: After sorting bottle caps into two piles, ask: 'Why do these belong together?'
steps: Sort a pile of objects into two groups using a rule you have not been told yet.
Ask yourself, 'Why do these belong together?' and look closely before answering.
Helps you turn their answer into one short sentence, such as 'They are all round.'

methods.title: What Makes a Set
methods.example: All the round buttons in one pile are a set because they share the same shape.
steps: Place a mixed group of objects, such as stones and shells, in front of you.
Pick out a small group that shares one feature, such as colour or size, and call it a set.
Find one more object from the pile that belongs in the same set.

methods.title: Counting How Many Are in Each Set
methods.example: Count the brown beans one by one: 1, 2, 3, 4 — there are 4 brown beans.
steps: After sorting objects into two sets, touch each object in the first set once while counting aloud.
Say the total number out loud, such as 'This set has 6.'
Count the second set the same way and say its total too.

methods.title: Comparing Two Sets
methods.example: 5 dates is more than 3 dates, so the date pile has more.
steps: Line the two sets up side by side and match one object from each set into pairs.
Look for the set with objects left over that have no pair.
Say out loud which set has more and which has fewer, pointing at the leftover objects as proof.

methods.title: Sorting the Same Objects a New Way
methods.example: Sort buttons by colour first, then mix them and sort the very same buttons by size.
steps: Sort a pile of objects by one rule, such as colour, and name the two sets together.
Mix all the objects back into one pile.
Sort the very same objects again using a new rule, such as size, and compare the new sets to the first ones.

workedExamples.title: Sorting Bottle Caps by Colour
workedExamples.prompt: Amina has 6 bottle caps: 4 are red and 2 are blue. Sort them into two sets using the rule 'red / not red'.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at each bottle cap one at a time. Step 2: Put every red cap into the 'red' pile. Step 3: Put the blue caps into the 'not red' pile. Step 4: Check — the red pile has 4 caps and the not-red pile has 2 caps.

workedExamples.title: Naming the Sorting Rule
workedExamples.prompt: Hodan sorted her stones into two piles: smooth stones and rough stones. What rule did she use, and how would she explain it?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look closely at what is the same about the stones in each pile. Step 2: Notice one pile feels smooth and the other feels rough. Step 3: Say the rule in a full sentence: 'I sorted the stones by how they feel — smooth or rough.'

workedExamples.title: Is This a Set?
workedExamples.prompt: Look at three shells that are all small and all white. Are they a set? Explain why.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Check what the three shells have in common. Step 2: Notice they are all small and all white. Step 3: Say yes — they are a set, because a set is a group of things that belong together, and these shells share size and colour.

workedExamples.title: Counting Each Set of Buttons
workedExamples.prompt: There are 5 blue buttons and 3 yellow buttons on the mat. How many buttons are in each set?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Touch each blue button once while counting: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Step 2: Touch each yellow button once while counting: 1, 2, 3. Step 3: Say the totals out loud: the blue set has 5 and the yellow set has 3.

workedExamples.title: Which Set of Dates Has More?
workedExamples.prompt: One plate has 7 dates. Another plate has 4 dates. Which plate has more, and which has fewer?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Count the dates on each plate: 7 and 4. Step 2: Match one date from each plate into pairs until one plate runs out. Step 3: The plate with 7 dates has 3 left over with no pair, so it has more. Step 4: Say it out loud: '7 is more than 4, so the first plate has more and the second plate has fewer.'

workedExamples.title: Sorting the Same Beans Two Ways
workedExamples.prompt: You have 8 dried beans, some big and some small, some brown and some white. First sort them by size. Then sort the very same beans by colour.
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Sort the 8 beans into 'big' and 'small' piles and count each pile. Step 2: Mix all 8 beans back together. Step 3: Now sort the very same beans into 'brown' and 'white' piles. Step 4: Notice the piles look different this time, because the same objects can be sorted in more than one way.

workedExamples.title: Building a Sorting Circle
workedExamples.prompt: Make one circle with string on the mat. The rule is 'toys'. Where do a toy car, a spoon, and a toy ball go?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Remember that things which fit the rule go inside the circle and things that do not fit stay outside. Step 2: The toy car fits the rule 'toys', so it goes inside. Step 3: The toy ball also fits, so it goes inside. Step 4: The spoon is not a toy, so it stays outside the circle.

workedExamples.title: First Steps with Two Circles
workedExamples.prompt: Draw two overlapping circles with string: one for 'toys' and one for 'red things'. Where does a red toy teddy go?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Check if the teddy fits only one rule or both. Step 2: The teddy is a toy, so it fits the 'toys' circle. Step 3: The teddy is also red, so it fits the 'red things' circle too. Step 4: Because it fits both rules, the teddy goes in the middle, where the two circles overlap.

workedExamples.title: Sorting a Bigger Pile by One Rule
workedExamples.prompt: Faarax has 10 mixed buttons: some are big, some are small. He wants to sort them using one rule of his own choosing. What could his rule be, and how would he sort?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at the pile and notice what is different about the buttons, such as size. Step 2: Choose one clear rule, for example 'big / not big'. Step 3: Sort all 10 buttons into the two piles using that one rule, checking each button carefully. Step 4: Count each pile to see how many fit the rule and how many do not.

workedExamples.title: Spotting the Wrong Rule
workedExamples.prompt: Layla says her rule for sorting stones was 'round', but her 'round' pile has one square stone in it. What went wrong, and how should she fix it?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Look at every stone in the 'round' pile one at a time. Step 2: Find the square stone — it does not match the rule 'round'. Step 3: Move the square stone out of that pile and into the 'not round' pile instead. Step 4: Explain the mistake: 'This stone is square, not round, so it belongs in the other pile.'

workedExamples.title: Choosing What Belongs in a Set
workedExamples.prompt: The set is 'red fruits'. Here are four items: a red apple, a green mango, a red tomato, and a blue cup. Which items belong in the set?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Read the rule for the set: it must be red and a fruit. Step 2: Check the red apple — it is red and a fruit, so it belongs. Step 3: Check the red tomato — it is red and often used as a fruit in cooking, so it belongs too. Step 4: The green mango is not red, and the blue cup is not a fruit, so neither belongs in the set.

workedExamples.title: Counting a Scattered Set
workedExamples.prompt: 9 stones are scattered all over the mat, not in a neat line. How can you count them accurately without missing any or counting one twice?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1: Move each stone into a single pile or line as you count it, so counted stones are separated from uncounted ones. Step 2: Touch each stone once and say the next number: 1, 2, 3, and so on. Step 3: Stop when every stone has been moved and counted. Step 4: Say the final total out loud: 'There are 9 stones.'

practice.prompt: Sort these 6 bottle caps: 4 are silver and 2 are gold. Put them into two sets — 'silver' and 'not silver'.
practice.answer: The silver set has 4 bottle caps and the not-silver (gold) set has 2 bottle caps.
practice.hint: Look at each cap and decide if it matches the rule 'silver' before placing it.

practice.prompt: You have 5 dried dates and 3 dried beans mixed together. Sort them into 'dates' and 'not dates'.
practice.answer: 5 dates go in the 'dates' set and 3 beans go in the 'not dates' set.
practice.hint: Pick up each object and ask, 'Is this a date?' before placing it.

practice.prompt: Look at a pile with 4 round stones and 2 square stones. Which rule could sort them into two clear sets?
practice.answer: The rule 'round / not round' sorts them into a set of 4 round stones and a set of 2 not-round (square) stones.
practice.hint: Notice the shape of each stone before deciding which pile it belongs in.

practice.prompt: A set of goats has 7 goats and a set of chickens has 3 chickens. How many animals are in each set?
practice.answer: The goat set has 7 animals and the chicken set has 3 animals.
practice.hint: Count each set separately by touching one animal at a time.

practice.prompt: Count the buttons in this set: 🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘 (5 buttons). How many buttons are in the set?
practice.hint: Touch each button once and say the number as you go.

practice.prompt: Count the shells in this set: 🐚🐚🐚🐚🐚🐚🐚 (7 shells). How many shells are in the set?
practice.hint: Point to each shell only once while counting aloud.

practice.prompt: One set has 8 stars and another set has 5 stars. Which set has more?
practice.answer: The set with 8 stars has more; the set with 5 stars has fewer.
practice.hint: Match the stars from each set into pairs to see which set has leftovers.

practice.prompt: There are 6 cups and 9 plates on the table. Are there more cups or more plates?
practice.answer: There are more plates (9) than cups (6); the cups are fewer.
practice.hint: Compare the two totals — the bigger number has more.

practice.prompt: True or false: 'The same pile of buttons can only ever be sorted one way.' Circle the word that is true.
practice.answer: False — the same pile can be sorted in more than one way, such as by colour or by size.
practice.hint: Think about sorting the same buttons first by colour, then by size.

practice.prompt: A group of 8 sandals is compared with a group of 5 sandals. Are there more in the first group or the second group?
practice.answer: The first group (8 sandals) has more; the second group (5 sandals) has fewer.
practice.hint: Line the sandals up in pairs to see which group has extras left over.

practice.prompt: A Venn circle is drawn for 'fruit'. A mango, a stone, and a banana are placed near it. Which ones go inside the circle?
practice.answer: The mango and the banana go inside the circle because they are fruit; the stone stays outside because it is not fruit.
practice.hint: Ask if each object fits the rule 'fruit' before placing it.

practice.prompt: Two circles overlap: one for 'red things', one for 'toys'. A red toy ball, a blue toy car, and a red cup are sorted. Where does each one go?
practice.answer: The red toy ball goes in the middle (it is both red and a toy). The blue toy car goes only in the 'toys' circle. The red cup goes only in the 'red things' circle.
practice.hint: Check each object against both rules before deciding where it belongs.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.title: What This Unit Is About: Sorting and Comparing
rules.text: Unit 7 is your first taste of statistics – the maths of organising and comparing information. At this age that means three friendly ideas: sorting objects into groups called sets, comparing sets to say which has more or fewer, and using a simple Venn diagram (sorting circles) to show what belongs together. There are no big numbers here. The whole unit is about looking carefully, noticing what is the same and what is different, and explaining a sorting rule out loud.

rules.title: Sorting Objects Into Two Sets by One Rule
rules.text: Sort a group of objects into two sets using one rule (for example red / not red).

rules.title: How to Teach It: Sorting a Pile by One Rule
rules.text: How to teach it: Tip a small pile of buttons onto a mat. Say, ‘Let us put all the red ones here and all the not-red ones here.’ Move the first two or three yourself, thinking out loud, then continue. When they finish, ask the key question: ‘Why do these belong together?’ Getting you to say the rule – ‘they are all red’ – matters more than the sorting itself. Always sort into two sets first: the things that fit the rule, and the things that do not (‘red’ and ‘not red’). This ‘something / not something’ pairing is the clearest way in for a five-year-old.

rules.title: Sorting rules are a choice
rules.text: One powerful idea to plant gently: the same objects can be sorted in more than one way. Sort the buttons by colour, then sweep them back together and sort the very same buttons by size. You begins to see that a sorting rule is a choice, not a fixed property of the objects. This is a genuinely important mathematical idea and children find it delightful once they notice it.

rules.title: The Venn Diagram — One Sorting Circle
rules.text: A Venn diagram is just a sorting circle. Things that fit the rule go inside the circle; things that do not fit stay outside. Because you have already been sorting into ‘something / not something’, a one-circle Venn diagram is a small, natural step: the circle is the ‘something’ pile, and outside is the ‘not something’ pile.

rules.title: How to Teach It: Two Overlapping Circles and 'Both'
rules.text: How to teach it: Start by placing objects that clearly fit only one circle – a blue car is a toy but not red, an apple is red but not a toy. Then bring out the red teddy and ask, ‘This is a toy AND it is red. Where can it go?’ puzzle over it, then show how the overlapping middle solves the problem. Objects that fit neither rule (a green cup) go outside both circles. Keep to a few very clear objects. The aim is only that you meet the idea that the middle means ‘both’; deep mastery comes in later years.

terms: Put objects into groups by a rule
Look at two sets side by side
Fits the rule / does not fit
Fits two rules at once (the middle)
commonMistakes: A common mistake is putting a peg in the wrong pile by its colour instead of its material
For example, placing a wooden peg that is painted white into the plastic pile. Remember the rule is about material (wooden or plastic), not colour, and check each peg by touch.
A common mistake is naming the rule too vaguely, such as just saying 'these are good ones,' without explaining the actual sorting feature
Say exactly what makes the oranges the same — their size.
A common mistake is sorting by size instead of by bread type, putting a large piece of sabaayad into the anjero pile because it looks similar in size
Remember to check what kind of bread it is, not how big the piece is.
A common mistake is sorting by colour instead of material, putting a clear plastic cup into the glass pile because it looks see-through
Remember the rule is about material (plastic or glass), and tap or feel the cup to check.
A common mistake is assuming one set must have more just because it looks bigger in the drawer
Count both sets carefully — here they are equal, with 5 in each.

fluency.prompt: Sort 5 buttons: 3 red and 2 blue, using the rule 'red / not red'. How many are red?
fluency.hint: Check each button's colour before placing it in a pile.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting the blue buttons instead of the red ones. Point to the red pile only and recount: 1, 2, 3.

fluency.prompt: A pile is sorted into 'wooden spoons' and 'metal spoons'. What is the sorting rule?
fluency.answer: The rule is what the spoon is made of — wooden or metal.
fluency.hint: Think about what makes the two piles different from each other.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is describing the rule by size or colour instead of material. Ask, 'What are they made of?' to back to the correct rule.

fluency.prompt: Are 3 red apples on a plate a set? Explain your answer.
fluency.answer: Yes, they are a set because they all share the same colour and are the same kind of fruit.
fluency.hint: Ask what all three apples have in common.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying they are not a set because they are different sizes. Remember a set only needs one shared rule (here, being red apples), not identical size.

fluency.prompt: Count this set of stones: 🪨🪨🪨🪨🪨🪨 (6 stones). How many stones are there?
fluency.hint: Touch each stone once as you count.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is skipping a stone or counting one twice. Have you move each stone to a new pile as it is counted.

fluency.prompt: One set has 9 dates, another has 6 dates. Which set has fewer?
fluency.answer: The set with 6 dates has fewer.
fluency.hint: Compare the two numbers — the smaller number has fewer.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is picking the set with 9 as 'fewer' by mixing up more and fewer. Remember that a smaller number means fewer.

fluency.prompt: The same 6 buttons are sorted by colour, then sorted again by size. Will the two sortings look the same or different?
fluency.answer: They will usually look different, because sorting by colour groups them one way and sorting by size groups them another way.
fluency.hint: Think about whether colour and size always match up in the same objects.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is assuming the piles must look identical every time. Look at both sortings side by side to see the difference.

fluency.prompt: A circle is drawn for the rule 'yellow things'. Does a yellow banana go inside or outside the circle?
fluency.answer: Inside, because a yellow banana fits the rule 'yellow things'.
fluency.hint: Check whether the object matches the rule written for the circle.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is placing the banana outside because it is a fruit, not thinking about its colour. Remember the rule here is about colour, not what kind of object it is.

fluency.prompt: Two circles overlap: 'round things' and 'yellow things'. Where does a round yellow ball go?
fluency.answer: It goes in the middle, because it is both round and yellow.
fluency.hint: Check the object against both rules — does it fit one, or both?
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is placing the ball in only one circle. Ask, 'Is it round? Is it also yellow?' — since both are true, it belongs in the overlapping middle.

fluency.prompt: You gather 6 dried beans for sorting: 4 are brown and 2 are white. Sort them by colour. How many are in each set?
fluency.answer: 4 beans are in the brown set and 2 beans are in the white set.
fluency.hint: Separate the beans by colour first, then count each pile one at a time.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is losing track and counting a bean twice. Have you move each counted bean to a new spot so none are recounted.

fluency.prompt: From a mixed pile of 15 objects (buttons, dates, and stones), you pick out only the buttons and find there are 7 of them. How many of the 15 objects are buttons?
fluency.hint: Look at each object and set aside only the ones that are buttons before counting.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting stones or dates by accident along with the buttons. Remember to check each object's type before adding it to the count.

fluency.prompt: 10 mixed shells are sorted by the rule 'striped / not striped': 6 are striped and 4 are not. How many are in the 'not striped' set?
fluency.answer: 4 shells are in the 'not striped' set.
fluency.hint: Look for stripe patterns on each shell before placing it in a pile.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting the striped shells when asked about the 'not striped' set. Point only at the non-striped pile and recount.

fluency.prompt: A pile is sorted into 'big shapes' and 'small shapes'. What is the rule, and how could you say it to someone else?
fluency.answer: The rule is size — you would say, 'I sorted the shapes by size: big shapes in this pile, small shapes in that pile.'
fluency.hint: Notice what is the same about every shape within one pile.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is describing the rule using shape type (circle/square) instead of size. Compare sizes across the piles, not shapes.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Amina has 9 clothes pegs: 5 are wooden and 4 are plastic. She wants to sort them using one rule. Sort the pegs and say how many are in each set.
realProblems.answer: 5 wooden pegs go in one set and 4 plastic pegs go in the other set.
realProblems.hint: Pick up each peg and feel whether it is wooden or plastic before placing it.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is putting a peg in the wrong pile by its colour instead of its material — for example, placing a wooden peg that is painted white into the plastic pile. Remember the rule is about material (wooden or plastic), not colour, and check each peg by touch.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, Hodan sorted oranges into two baskets and says her rule is 'big oranges'. One basket has 6 big oranges and the other has 4 small oranges. How would Hodan explain her rule to a customer?
realProblems.answer: Hodan should say: 'I sorted the oranges by size — the big ones are in this basket, and the small ones are in that basket.'
realProblems.hint: Ask what is the same about all the oranges in the first basket before explaining.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is naming the rule too vaguely, such as just saying 'these are good ones,' without explaining the actual sorting feature. Say exactly what makes the oranges the same — their size.

realProblems.prompt: While travelling, the family sees a group of 4 goats standing together and 1 donkey standing apart. Is the group of 4 goats a set? Why or why not?
realProblems.answer: Yes, the 4 goats are a set because they are all the same kind of animal and belong together; the donkey is not part of that set because it is a different animal.
realProblems.hint: Ask what all the goats have in common that the donkey does not share.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying the donkey belongs in the set too because it is 'also an animal'. The rule for this set is specifically 'goats', so a different animal like a donkey does not belong. Point back to the rule and check each animal against it.

realProblems.prompt: Before dinner, there are 7 pieces of anjero and 3 pieces of sabaayad on a tray. Sort the bread using the rule 'anjero / not anjero'. How many are in each set?
realProblems.answer: 7 pieces of anjero go in the 'anjero' set and 3 pieces of sabaayad go in the 'not anjero' set.
realProblems.hint: Look closely at the shape of each piece of bread before deciding which set it belongs to.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is sorting by size instead of by bread type, putting a large piece of sabaayad into the anjero pile because it looks similar in size. Remember to check what kind of bread it is, not how big the piece is.

realProblems.prompt: There are 8 plastic cups and 2 glass cups on the shelf. Sort them using the rule 'plastic / not plastic' and say which set has more.
realProblems.answer: 8 plastic cups go in one set and 2 glass cups go in the other; the plastic set has more.
realProblems.hint: Tap each cup gently to check if it feels like plastic or glass before sorting it.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is sorting by colour instead of material, putting a clear plastic cup into the glass pile because it looks see-through. Remember the rule is about material (plastic or glass), and tap or feel the cup to check.

realProblems.prompt: In the evening, 5 spoons and 5 forks are mixed in a drawer. Sort them using the rule 'spoon / not spoon'. Are the two sets equal, more, or fewer?
realProblems.answer: 5 spoons go in one set and 5 forks go in the other set; the two sets have the same number, so neither has more.
realProblems.hint: Count each set carefully after sorting to compare them.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is assuming one set must have more just because it looks bigger in the drawer. Count both sets carefully — here they are equal, with 5 in each.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: You sorted 8 buttons into two piles using the rule 'shiny / not shiny'. Explain how you decided which pile each button belonged to.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: I looked at each button one at a time and checked if it was shiny. If it was shiny, I put it in the shiny pile — if it was not shiny, I put it in the other pile. This way, I sorted the group into two sets using one rule.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how you would compare a set of 6 stones and a set of 9 stones to say which has more.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: First I would count each set: 6 stones in one and 9 in the other. Then I would match the stones into pairs, one from each set. The set of 9 would have 3 stones left over with no pair, so I know 9 is more and 6 is fewer.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A friend says two sets can never be compared unless they have the same kind of object in them. Explain why this is or is not true, using an example.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: This is not true. You can compare any two sets by counting how many are in each, even if the objects are different — for example, comparing 4 goats to 7 chickens. Four is fewer than seven, so the goats are fewer, even though goats and chickens are different animals.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Two Circles and the Middle (‘both’).
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: This is the newest and trickiest idea, so treat it as a gentle first taste rather than something to master. Make two circles that overlap with two loops of string. One circle is for ‘toys’, the other for ‘red things’. An object that is a toy and red – a red teddy – belongs in the middle, where the circles overlap, because it fits both rules at once. Start by placing objects that clearly fit only one circle – a blue car is a toy but not red, an apple is red but not a toy. Then bring out the red teddy and ask, ‘This is a toy AND it is red — where can it go?’ puzzle over it, then show how the overlapping middle solves the problem, because the teddy fits both rules at once.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Unit 7 is your first taste.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Unit 7 is your first taste of statistics – the maths of organising and comparing information. At this age that means three friendly ideas: sorting objects into groups called sets, comparing sets to say which has more or fewer, and using a simple Venn diagram (sorting circles) to show what belongs together. There are no big numbers here. The whole unit is about looking carefully, noticing what is the same and what is different, and explaining a sorting rule out loud.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Sort a group of objects into two.
